content.text: What is the purpose of the spring in the galvanometer?
To ensure a uniform force on the coil
To complete the circuit through the coil
To counteract the motor effect on the coil
To increase the magnetic flux through the coil
A current-carrying coil in a magnetic field is pushed sideways by the motor effect. Ask what would happen to the pointer if nothing opposed that push.
A spring attached to the pointer provides a restoring torque, so the deflection settles at a value proportional to the current instead of increasing without limit.
The spring carries no current and sits outside the coil, so it can do nothing to the current or to the flux linking the coil.
C

When a current flows, the coil experiences a turning effect (the motor effect) that rotates it and moves the pointer. The spring is attached to the pointer and exerts a restoring torque that opposes this rotation, so the deflection is proportional to the current rather than increasing without limit. The spring does not carry current and does not change the flux linking the coil.

content.text: The diagram shows an apparatus that can be used to investigate properties of crystals.

content.alt_text: Diagram of a Bragg X-ray diffraction apparatus: an X-ray tube on the left, a collimator formed by two grey blocks, a beam of X-rays travelling right to an angled crystal, a diffracted ray going up to a detector, and a curved arrow showing the detector can swing through an arc. All parts are labelled.

content.text: What can scientists investigate about crystals using this apparatus?
How well crystals reflect X-rays
How the atoms in crystals are arranged
Whether crystals exhibit the property of superconductivity
Whether the electrical resistance of crystals is increased by impurities
The planes of atoms inside the crystal act like the lines of a diffraction grating, so the angles at which the X-rays emerge depend on the spacing between those planes.
Measuring the diffraction angle and using Bragg's law $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$ gives the plane spacing $d$, which is a statement about how the atoms are arranged.
None of these measurements depends on how strongly the crystal reflects the beam, nor on its electrical conductivity or critical temperature.
B

The Braggs directed X-rays at a crystal and measured the angles at which the diffracted beams appeared, obtaining the well-known Bragg relationship $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$. Because the diffraction angle depends on the spacing $d$ between the atomic planes, the measurements revealed the arrangement and spacing of atoms within the crystal. The apparatus gives no information about reflectivity alone, superconductivity or resistance.

items: 1 mark: selects option B - the Braggs determined how the atoms in crystals are arranged

content.text: Which of the following statements CANNOT be inferred from observations made when using the apparatus shown?
Cathode rays possess energy.
Cathode rays possess momentum.
Cathode rays travel in straight lines.
Cathode rays cannot pass through metals.
List the observations this apparatus actually supports: the shadow cast by the Maltese cross, what the paddle wheel does, and what the beam does in electric and magnetic fields.
A statement about momentum would need the beam's deflection under a known force, or the transfer of momentum to the paddle wheel - neither of which is measured here.
Penetration is one of the things this tube does demonstrate: the beam passes through a thin metal foil to light the screen behind it.
B

The Maltese cross experiment shows that cathode rays are particles, that they travel in straight lines, and that they are very penetrating (they can pass through thin metal foils); the paddle wheel being driven shows that they carry energy. None of these observations measures the momentum of the cathode rays, and the direction of travel is unchanged in an electric field, so no momentum information can be deduced from the observations made with this apparatus.

content.text: Gravity is the only force, so the horizontal velocity is constant and the horizontal gap between successive dots must be identical in every interval.

content.text: Why does the electrical resistance of a metal increase as temperature increases?
Lattice vibrations increase, scattering more electrons.
Electrons pair up, increasing their interactions with the crystal lattice.
Fewer electrons are free to move, as they fill the holes in the conduction band.
Electrons move more freely through the metal, unimpeded by the crystal lattice.
The number of conduction electrons in a metal changes very little with temperature, so the resistance must change because the electrons move less easily.
As the metal heats up the ions in the lattice vibrate more violently, so a conduction electron collides with them more often.
More scattering means a smaller drift velocity for the same electric field, and since $R = \dfrac{mv_d}{ne^{2}A}$ a smaller drift velocity means a larger resistance.
A

In a metal the ions in the lattice are vibrating about fixed positions. As the temperature rises these lattice vibrations become more violent, so the mobile conduction electrons collide with the ions more often and are scattered more frequently. Since the number of conduction electrons is essentially unchanged, the increased scattering reduces the drift velocity for a given field and hence increases the resistance.

items: 1 mark: selects option A - increased lattice vibrations scatter more electrons

content.text: Which of the following is a true statement about scientific theories, such as Einstein's theory of special relativity?
They are valid but unreliable ideas.
They are useful in making predictions.
They are concepts that lack an experimental basis.
They are ideas that can't be accepted until they have been tested.
A theory is not a guess. It is a set of ideas that has been tested repeatedly and has survived those tests.

The real test of a theory is whether its quantitative predictions can be checked by experiment - special relativity predicted time dilation, which has since been confirmed by atomic clocks flown around the world.
Reject any option that describes a theory as untested, unreliable, or as having no experimental basis.
B

A theory is not a guess: it is a well-supported explanation that has survived repeated experimental testing and that generates quantitative predictions which can be checked by experiment. Special relativity, for example, predicted the time dilation of muon lifetimes and has been confirmed by atomic clocks flown around the world. A theory is neither unreliable (A) nor untested (D), and option C contradicts the evidence base.

content.text: A current-carrying wire is placed perpendicular to a magnetic field.
Which graph correctly shows the relationship between magnetic field strength (B) and current (I) if the force is to remain constant?

content.alt_text: Graph of current I on the vertical axis against magnetic field strength B on the horizontal axis, showing an increasing curve that becomes progressively steeper (convex upwards).
Graph of current I on the vertical axis against magnetic field strength B on the horizontal axis, showing an increasing straight line through the origin.
Graph of current I on the vertical axis against magnetic field strength B on the horizontal axis, showing a decreasing curve that falls away more and more steeply at low B (inverse relationship).
Graph of current I on the vertical axis against magnetic field strength B on the horizontal axis, showing a decreasing straight line.

content.text: For a wire perpendicular to the field there is no trigonometry to do: $F = BIL\sin 90^{\circ} = BIL$.
Keeping $F$ and $L$ constant means the product $IB$ must stay constant, so $I \propto \dfrac{1}{B}$.
That is a rectangular hyperbola: very steep at small $B$ and flattening off as $B$ increases, which rules out the straight lines and the increasing curve.
C

For a wire perpendicular to the field, $F = BIL$, so keeping $F$ constant requires $IB = $ constant, i.e. $I \propto 1/B$. The graph of $I$ against $B$ must therefore be a decreasing rectangular hyperbola that is very steep at small $B$ and flattens as $B$ increases, which is graph C.

items: 1 mark: selects option C - the inverse $I$ versus $B$ relationship from $F = BIL$ held constant

content.text: In which of the following situations does the magnetic field exert the greatest force on the proton (p+), given that all of the fields are of equal magnitude?

content.alt_text: A proton shown as a grey dot inside a region of crosses (magnetic field into the page) with the label v = 0 and no velocity arrow.
A proton as a grey dot between two horizontal field lines arrowed to the right and labelled B, with a velocity arrow to the right and v = 60 m s-1; the velocity is parallel to the field.
A proton as a grey dot in a field of dots (magnetic field out of the page) with a velocity arrow pointing left and v = 40 m s-1; the velocity is perpendicular to the field.
A proton as a grey dot between two horizontal field lines arrowed to the right and labelled B, with a velocity arrow at 45 degrees to the field and v = 50 m s-1.

content.text: The magnitude of the force is $F = qvB\sin\theta$, where $\theta$ is the angle between the velocity and the field - identify $\theta$ in each diagram before comparing anything.
Two of the situations give zero force: a stationary charge feels no magnetic force, and neither does a charge moving along the field lines.
For the two that remain, calculate $v\sin\theta$ - the speeds are printed on the diagrams, so compare $40$ with $50\sin 45^{\circ}$ rather than comparing the speeds alone.
C

The force on a moving charge is $F = qvB\sin\theta$. In A the proton is stationary so $F = 0$. In B the velocity is parallel to the field so $\theta = 0$ and again $F = 0$. In D the velocity makes a $45^\circ$ angle with the field, giving $F \propto \sin 45^\circ = 0.71$. In C the velocity is perpendicular to the field, so $\sin\theta = 1$, and with a larger speed than D ($40$ against $50$ is close, but the sine factor dominates) the force is greatest. Graph C is the only case with the maximum value of $\sin\theta$.

items: 1 mark: selects option C - the velocity is perpendicular to the field so $F = qvB$ is maximised

content.text: P, Q and R are straight, current-carrying conductors. They all carry currents of the same magnitude (I). Conductors P and Q are fixed in place. The magnitude of the force between conductors Q and R is F newtons.

content.alt_text: Three vertical parallel conductors labelled P, Q and R separated by 10 mm and 10 mm. The current in P is downwards, the current in Q is upwards and the current in R is downwards, each marked I.

content.text: What is the net force on conductor R when it is in the position shown?
$\frac{F}{2}$ newtons to the left
$\frac{F}{2}$ newtons to the right
$\frac{3F}{2}$ newtons to the left
$\frac{3F}{2}$ newtons to the right
Parallel currents in the *same* direction attract; parallel currents in *opposite* directions repel. Check the direction of the current in each wire against the one in R.
The force per unit length between parallel conductors varies as $F \propto \dfrac{1}{d}$ - note that this is *not* the inverse square law.
P is twice as far from R as Q is, so find both force magnitudes and then add them with their directions before reading the options.
B

Parallel currents in the same direction attract and currents in opposite directions repel. R carries current downwards, the same direction as P (20 mm away) and opposite to Q (10 mm away). The repulsive force from Q, of magnitude $F$, acts on R to the right, while the attractive force from P, of magnitude $F\left(\frac{10}{20}\right)^{2} = \frac{F}{4}$, acts to the left. The resultant is therefore to the right, which corresponds to option B.

items: 1 mark: selects option B - a net force on R directed to the right

content.text: Which of the following represents a doped semiconductor?

content.alt_text: Square lattice of silicon atoms labelled Si joined by bonds, with one phosphorus atom labelled P replacing a silicon atom and a single free electron drawn just above and to the right of the P atom.
Square lattice of silicon atoms labelled Si with carbon atoms labelled C replacing some silicon atoms, and no free charge carriers shown.
Square lattice of silicon atoms labelled Si with one germanium atom labelled Ge replacing a silicon atom, and no free charge carriers shown.
Square lattice of silicon atoms labelled Si with one carbon atom labelled C replacing a silicon atom.

content.text: Doping means deliberately adding a small number of impurity atoms, usually from the group immediately above or below the host element in the periodic table.
Count valence electrons: a dopant with one more (or one fewer) than the host leaves a spare electron (or a hole) free to move through the lattice.
The correct diagram must actually show a free charge carrier. A group IV atom (C or Ge) substituted for silicon has the same number of valence electrons, so it produces none.
A

Doping a semiconductor means deliberately adding a small number of impurity atoms. Group V elements such as phosphorus have five valence electrons, so when a P atom replaces a Si atom in the lattice it contributes a fifth bonding electron which is not needed for a bond and becomes a delocalised free electron in the conduction band. That is exactly what lattice A shows. Carbon and germanium are group IV, so lattices B, C and D have the same number of valence electrons as silicon and produce no free carriers, which is why they are not doped semiconductors.

items: 1 mark: selects option A - a group V dopant (P) providing a free electron in the conduction band

content.text: Which of the following diagrams correctly represents the force(s) acting on a satellite in a stable circular orbit around Earth?
Key: $F_g$ = gravitational force, $F_p$ = propulsive force, $F_c$ = centripetal force, $F_r$ = reaction force.
In each diagram the small object is a satellite and the large sphere is the Earth.

content.alt_text: Satellite above the Earth showing a force arrow Fg pointing straight down towards the centre of the Earth and a force arrow Fp pointing down and to the right.
Satellite above the Earth showing a force arrow Fg pointing straight down, a force arrow Fp pointing down and to the right, and a force arrow Fc pointing up and to the right.
Satellite above the Earth showing a single force arrow Fg pointing straight down towards the centre of the Earth.
Satellite above the Earth showing a single force arrow Fg pointing straight down, angled slightly towards the centre of the Earth.

content.text: A satellite in a stable circular orbit is coasting: its speed is not changing, so no thrust is needed to hold it there.
The centripetal force is not an extra force - it is the name for the *net* force directed at the centre, and the reaction force in Newton's third law acts on the Earth, not on the satellite.
So the satellite should show exactly one arrow, and it must lie along the line joining the satellite to the centre of the Earth, not vertically down the page.
D

A satellite in a stable circular orbit is coasting: no thrust is required to maintain the orbit, so there is no propulsive force, and Newton's third law does not create a separate 'reaction' force on the satellite because the reaction acts on the Earth. The only force on the satellite is its weight $F_g$, which is directed at the centre of the Earth and so acts as the centripetal force. Diagram D shows exactly this single force directed towards the centre.

items: 1 mark: selects option D - a single gravitational force directed towards the centre of the Earth (the centripetal force)

content.text: A simple AC generator was connected to a cathode ray oscilloscope and the coil was rotated at a constant rate. The output is shown on this graph.

content.alt_text: Graph of voltage against time for the generator output, with the vertical axis marked 1, 0 and -1 and a sinusoidal trace completing two full cycles between successive dashed vertical lines.

content.text: Which of the following graphs best represents the output if the rate of rotation is decreased to half of the original value?

content.alt_text: Graph of voltage against time showing four complete sinusoidal cycles between the dashed vertical lines, with the same peak amplitude as the original trace.
Graph of voltage against time showing four complete sinusoidal cycles between the dashed vertical lines, with a larger peak amplitude than the original trace.
Graph of voltage against time showing a single complete sinusoidal cycle between the dashed vertical lines.
Graph of voltage against time showing a single complete sinusoidal cycle between the dashed vertical lines, with the same peak amplitude as the original trace.

content.text: For a coil of $N$ turns and area $A$ rotating at angular speed $\omega$, the induced emf is $\varepsilon = NBA\sin(\omega t)$ - the rotation rate appears in *both* the period and the peak value.
Halving the rotation rate therefore doubles the period *and* halves the peak voltage, so look for a trace with half as many cycles per dashed interval and half the height.

Count the cycles between the dashed vertical lines and compare the peak height with the original trace before choosing; two of the options have the right number of cycles and differ only in amplitude.
D

The peak emf of a generator is proportional to the rate of rotation of the coil, so halving the rotation rate halves the frequency of the induced emf but leaves the amplitude unchanged. The original trace completes two cycles per dashed interval, so the new trace must complete one cycle per dashed interval with the same peak voltage. That is graph D.

items: 1 mark: selects option D - half the frequency with unchanged amplitude

content.text: Which material would absorb a photon of wavelength $8.60 \times 10^{-7}\,\mathrm{m}$, causing an electron to just jump the band gap?
Ge
Si
GaAs
$\mathrm{SiO_2}$
For the electron to *just* jump the gap, the photon energy must equal the band gap, so convert the wavelength into an energy in electronvolts.
$E = hf = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$ with $h = 6.63\times10^{-34}\,\mathrm{J\,s}$ and $c = 3.00\times10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, then divide by $1.60\times10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$ per electronvolt.
Read the four gap values off the diagram and match the calculated energy against them.
C

The photon energy is $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{6.63 \times 10^{-34} \times 3.00 \times 10^{8}}{8.60 \times 10^{-7}} = 2.31 \times 10^{-19}\,\mathrm{J}$, which is $\dfrac{2.31 \times 10^{-19}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} \approx 1.44\,\mathrm{eV}$. For the electron to just jump the band gap, the photon energy must equal the gap, and the only material with a gap of about $1.43\,\mathrm{eV}$ is GaAs.

items: 1 mark: selects option C - GaAs, whose band gap of 1.43 eV matches the photon energy of about 1.44 eV

content.text: A passenger is playing billiards on a train that is travelling forwards on a level track. The ball takes the path shown when hit by the cue.

content.alt_text: Plan view of a billiards table inside a moving train, with an arrow labelled Front of train pointing to the left. A cue strikes a ball that is initially at rest; a dotted path curves to the right and forward from the initial position of the ball to a later position of the ball.

content.text: What can be inferred about the motion of the train?
It is turning left.
It is speeding up.
It is turning right.
It is slowing down.
After the strike the ball moves in a straight line at constant speed, since friction on the table is negligible.
If the path looks curved to a passenger on the train, the train's frame of reference is accelerating, so the train must be turning rather than speeding up or slowing down.
A free object in a turning vehicle appears to drift towards the *outside* of the turn, so the direction in which the path curves tells you which way the train is turning.
C

Once the cue strikes it the ball moves in a straight line at constant velocity, so relative to the train its path can only be straight. The path shown is curved, so the train's frame of reference is not inertial: the train must be turning, not speeding up or slowing down.

The arrow labelled 'Front of train' points to the left in this plan view, so the right-hand side of the train is the top of the page and its left-hand side is the bottom. The dotted path curves downwards, that is, towards the left-hand side of the train.

content.text: Astronauts travel at a velocity of $0.9c$ to Alpha Centauri. Newtonian physics predicts that this journey would take 4.86 years.
How many years will the journey take in the frame of reference of the astronauts?
The departure and the arrival happen at the same place in the astronauts' own frame, so the time they measure is the *proper* time - the shortest time between the two events.
$t = t_0\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}$ with $t_0 = 4.86$ years and $v = 0.9c$, so work out $\sqrt{1 - 0.9^{2}}$ before multiplying.
The longer value in the options is the dilated time measured in the Earth's frame, not the astronauts' time.

The 4.86 years is the time measured in the Earth's frame. The astronauts are in the frame in which the departure and arrival events occur at the same place, so they measure the proper time, $t = t_0\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}} = 4.86\sqrt{1 - 0.9^{2}} = 4.86 \times 0.436 = 2.12$ years. content.text: When the switch is closed, the pointer on the galvanometer deflects.
How could the size of the deflection be increased?

Decrease the number of secondary coils
Replace the iron core with a copper core

The deflection is caused by the emf induced in the *secondary* coil, so work out how that depends on the two sets of turns.
For an ideal transformer $\dfrac{V_p}{V_s} = \dfrac{N_p}{N_s}$, so $V_s = V_p\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$ - decide which of those two numbers you would increase.
The core has to carry a *changing* flux for anything to be induced, so a copper core would stop the transfer altogether, and a series resistor would reduce the current driving the coil.
A

For an ideal transformer $\dfrac{V_p}{V_s} = \dfrac{N_p}{N_s}$. The deflection of the galvanometer is set by the emf induced in the secondary coil, $V_s = V_p\dfrac{N_s}{N_p}$. Decreasing the number of primary turns while keeping the supply voltage and the number of secondary turns constant increases $V_s$ and hence the deflection. Decreasing the secondary turns or adding a series resistor would reduce it, and a copper core would not transmit the changing flux to the secondary at all.

content.text: An astronaut working outside a spacecraft in orbit around Earth is not attached to it.
Why does the astronaut NOT drift away from the spacecraft?
The force of gravity acting on the astronaut and spacecraft is negligible.
The spacecraft and the astronaut are in orbit around the Sun with the Earth.
The forces due to gravity acting on both the astronaut and the spacecraft are the same.
The accelerations of the astronaut and the spacecraft are inversely proportional to their respective masses.
Compare the accelerations of the astronaut and the spacecraft, not the forces on them - at orbital altitude the gravitational field is still strong.
Both bodies are at the same place, so they are in the same gravitational field and $a = \dfrac{F_g}{m} = \dfrac{GM}{r^{2}}$, which does not depend on the mass.
Since $F \propto m$, the larger body has the larger force but also the greater mass, so the two accelerations come out equal and the astronaut floats alongside.
D

At orbital altitude the gravitational force on each body is large, not negligible, so A is wrong. The two bodies orbit together, so B is irrelevant. The gravitational forces on the astronaut and the spacecraft are not equal because their masses differ, so C is wrong. Because both bodies are acted on by the same gravitational field they experience the same acceleration, $a = F/m = GM/r^{2}$, which is why the astronaut floats alongside the spacecraft instead of drifting away. Since $F \propto m$, the acceleration is inversely proportional to the mass. D was accepted as the best of the four alternatives.

At what angle to the horizontal was it launched?

Split the range and the time of flight into horizontal and vertical parts: $R = u\cos\theta\,t$ and $T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$.
Eliminate $u$ rather than solving for it: dividing one relation by the other gives $\tan\theta = \dfrac{gT^{2}}{2R}$.
Substitute $T = 3.5\,\mathrm{s}$ and $R = 70\,\mathrm{m}$ and compare the result with the angles offered.

Horizontally, $R = u\cos\theta\, t$, so $u\cos\theta = 70/3.5 = 20\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Vertically, $T = \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$, so $u\sin\theta = \dfrac{3.5 \times 9.8}{2} = 17.2\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$. Therefore $\tan\theta = 17.2/20 = 0.86$, giving $\theta = 40.6^\circ \approx 40^\circ$.

content.text: How is the direction of the torque maintained as the loop rotates $360^\circ$ from the position shown?
Track the loop through a half turn: the sides that experience the driving force change places, so on its own the torque would reverse.
The commutator is split into two halves, and each brush rests on a different half as the loop turns, so the connections swap automatically.
Explain how that current reversal keeps the torque pointing the same way, and why the swap must happen twice during a full $360^{\circ}$ rotation.
The split-ring commutator reverses the direction of the current in the loop every half turn, so the torque always acts in the same direction.

Initially the conventional current flows around the loop in the direction ABCD; after the loop has rotated through $90^\circ$ the split-ring commutator reverses the current so it flows DCBA. This reversal happens twice during a $360^\circ$ rotation, and each time the forces on the two active sides swap over, so the torque always acts in the same sense and the motor continues to turn in one direction.

content.text: In 1865, James Clerk Maxwell developed the theory of electromagnetism. This theory explained the nature of light. It also predicted the existence of other electromagnetic waves.
How did Hertz test and validate Maxwell's theory?

Begin with the prediction that needed testing. Maxwell claimed that light and other electromagnetic waves share the same nature, so the test was to produce waves that cannot be seen and then show they behave like light.

For generation and detection, think about the small gaps in Hertz's apparatus: what happens across a gap when a high voltage is applied, and what happens when a high-frequency wave arrives at a loop of wire.

For the validation, list the wave behaviours Hertz demonstrated, such as reflection, refraction and interference, and say how the speed he obtained confirmed that the waves he had generated were light.
Hertz generated and detected radio waves with a spark gap and a loop detector, showed they were reflected and refracted like light, and measured their speed as the speed of light.

Hertz performed a series of experiments designed to demonstrate the existence of 'invisible' electromagnetic waves (radio waves), that these waves behaved like visible light, and that their speed was the speed of light.

His basic design used a high voltage source to produce a spark, with a detector formed from a loop of copper wire with a small gap. Radio waves produced by the spark were detected when a tiny spark was induced across the gap in the detector.
Further experiments using reflecting surfaces and other apparatus showed that radio waves can be reflected and refracted, behaviours consistent with visible light.

A modification of the design allowed him to determine the velocity of the radio waves using an interference pattern to determine their wavelength; because the frequency was set by the high voltage source, $v = f\lambda$ could be used. The value obtained was the speed of light.
These experiments provided substantial experimental evidence supporting the predictions made by Maxwell, thus validating the theory.

content.text: On the axes, sketch the graph of the velocity of the trolley as it travels from A to D under the magnet, and justify your graph.

First mark the part of the journey over which the magnetic flux through the copper plate changes. Where the field of the magnet is negligible, nothing is induced and the trolley keeps a constant velocity.
Then decide which way the trolley is pushed. Induced currents oppose the change that produces them, by Lenz's law, so the force on the plate opposes the motion of the plate through the field.

Finally fix the shape of the falling section. The deceleration is greatest when the flux is changing fastest, which is when the plate is directly under the magnet, so the graph should steepen then flatten rather than fall in a straight line.
The velocity is constant from A to B, falls smoothly from $v_i$ to $v_f$ between B and C, and is constant at the lower value $v_f$ from C to D.
The velocity of the trolley is reduced as it passes through the region under the magnet (B to C) because its kinetic energy is transformed into heat energy in the copper plate.

This happens because of the flux change produced by the movement of the copper plate through the field of the strong magnet. This induces currents in the copper plate (Faraday's law) which produce a magnetic field that opposes the changing flux (Lenz's law) and hence produces a force that decelerates the trolley.

The graph is therefore flat at $v_i$ from A to B, curves down smoothly (slightly convex upward) from B to C as the rate of flux change is greatest when the plate is directly under the magnet, and is then flat at the lower value $v_f$ from C to D. Energy conservation requires $v_f < v_i$.

content.text: What are the advantages of using superconductors to produce the magnetic fields used to guide protons around the LHC?
What field strength is needed to hold protons moving at nearly the speed of light on a circular path, and how is that field produced? By the current in the magnet coils.
Then consider what limits the current in an ordinary magnet: the heating produced as charge is pushed through the resistance of the coil, $P = I^{2}R$.
Note both the field strength that becomes achievable and the practical consequence for the size of the machine, since that is an advantage a student could describe.
Superconductors allow very large currents with no resistive heating, so much stronger magnetic fields can be produced in a smaller magnet.
Strong magnetic fields are required to deflect the protons due to their high speeds and the effect of mass dilation - that is, the Lorentz factor by which their inertial mass exceeds their rest mass.

To produce strong fields, high currents are required in the magnet coils. A superconductor has zero resistance, so it carries those very high currents with no resistive heating ($P = I^{2}R = 0$) and no power loss in the coils. Superconducting magnets therefore sustain a much stronger field than an equivalent resistive magnet of the same size, which allows the LHC's bending magnets to be smaller and the ring to be more compact.

content.text: Explain how Newton's Laws of Motion and Universal Gravitation were applied to the Cassini mission.
Split the mission into three stages, launch, the long coast including the gravity assists, and the orbit achieved at Saturn, and decide which of Newton's laws is relevant to each stage.

Newton's third law powered the launch, Newton's second law governed its acceleration, the first law and the Law of Universal Gravitation governed the coast to Saturn and the gravity assists, and the Law of Universal Gravitation sets the stable orbit at Saturn.

Launching the probe from the surface of the Earth requires the application of Newton's third law in the operation of the rocket: exhaust gases are expelled downwards and hence apply an upwards force on the rocket. During launch, the acceleration of the vehicle is governed by the mass of the vehicle and the thrust of the engines as described by Newton's second law.

Newton's first law of motion is relevant during the journey to Saturn. The probe is travelling through space and so does not experience friction or air resistance, and so continues in its motion affected only by the gravity of the Sun, and hence by the Law of Universal Gravitation.
The slingshot effect utilises the law of gravitation as well as conservation of momentum (Newton's third law) to increase the velocity of the space probe.

A stable orbit around Saturn can be predicted using the law of gravitation: the orbital velocity and radius of the orbit are related by the balance between the gravitational force and the required centripetal force.

content.text: Part (i). The volume of each rock sample is the volume of water displaced, that is the difference between the final and initial readings. Since $1\,\mathrm{mL} = 1\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ the table volumes are already in $\mathrm{cm^3}$, matching the gram masses.

Basalt is therefore the denser of the two: $\dfrac{2.975}{2.64} = 1.13$, about 13% denser than granite, which is consistent with basalt being the mafic rock. The comparison is quantitative, which is what the question asks for.

Part (ii). Elasticity is measured by comparing the applied force with the resulting deformation, so two rocks of identical density can be distinguished by how stiff they are. Magnetism depends on the identity and quantity of magnetic minerals present, so it too varies between two rocks of the same density, and mapping how it varies is one of the ways a geophysicist infers what lies at depth. content.text: Earth's magnetic field is not constant over geological time.

Part (i): the word 'long-term' fixes the timescale at millions of years, so think about what the record shows about the positions of the magnetic poles over that period, and about what rock or sediment can preserve that record.

Part (ii): a magnetic field on Earth has to be produced by moving charge, so ask what in the interior is moving and how the pattern of that motion could change with time. There is more than one mechanism.
For part (ii), three marks need three causes or one developed cause plus a second. Look at the liquid outer core and at how it rotates relative to the crust.

items: Periodic magnetic reversals: the north and south magnetic poles swap over, at irregular intervals, many times in Earth's history. Slow drift of the pole positions across the globe - polar wandering - is also acceptable.

Convection currents in the liquid outer core and in the mantle change the flow of ionised material and hence the field, and the difference between the rotation rate of the liquid interior and that of the crust - which also varies with depth and latitude - changes the field further.

content.text: Part (i). The Earth's field is not static. The record shows that the geomagnetic north and south poles have repeatedly exchanged positions, at intervals that are irregular - hundreds of thousands of years apart on average - and many times over Earth's history. The gradual drift of the pole positions across the globe, polar wandering, is a related long-term change. Both are established from magnetised volcanic rocks and sediments, which record the direction of the field at the moment they cooled through their Curie temperature.

Part (ii). The field is produced by the movement of ionised material in the conducting liquid outer core. Convection cells in that liquid, and in the mantle, change the pattern and the rate of flow of the ions and therefore the current distribution and the field. In addition, the liquid interior does not rotate in step with the crust: the rotation rate differs, and it also varies with depth and with latitude, so this differential rotation changes the field. Axial tilt, the creation of new crust and the subduction of old crust all produce further long-term changes.

content.alt_text: Graph with depth in km on the horizontal axis from 2000 to 5000 and, on the left axis, P wave speed in km s-1 marked 5, 10 and 15, and, on the right axis, density in units of 10^3 kg m-3. A dashed curve shows P wave speed rising from about 8 to 14 km s-1 and dropping sharply at 2900 km, while a solid curve labelled Density rises slowly to 5 then jumps sharply to about 10 at 2900 km and rises steadily to 13 by 5000 km.

content.text: Part (i): restrict your attention to the depth range 3500 km to 4500 km and look only at the two curves over that interval. Ask whether their gradients there are the same or different, and ignore the sharp feature at about 2900 km, which lies outside the range.

Part (ii): the ray-path diagram shows three separate features of the P-wave paths - a curved path in the mantle, a partial reflection at a boundary, and a curved path in the outer core. Match each one to a change in the medium at that depth.

For each feature, name the property of the medium that changes and then say how the wave behaves because of it. Where the change is gradual the wave bends smoothly; where it is abrupt the wave splits into a reflected and a transmitted part.

items: P wave speed is directly proportional to density over that interval; both density and P wave speed rise steadily, at the same rate, between 3500 km and 4500 km.

The paths curve in the mantle because P wave speed increases with depth, so the waves refract continuously towards the normal; some waves are partly reflected at the mantle-outer core boundary because of the abrupt density change there; and in the outer core the waves refract again and follow a curved path, with the opposite sense of curvature, because density continues to increase with depth.

content.text: Part (i). Over the interval 3500 km to 4500 km both the solid density curve and the dashed P wave speed curve rise smoothly, with no change of gradient, so the two quantities are proportional there: the outer core is both denser and faster for P waves as depth increases. The sharp discontinuity at about 2900 km, the mantle-outer core boundary, is not in this range and does not affect the relationship being asked about.

Part (ii). In the mantle the P wave speed increases with depth, so a wave entering each deeper, faster layer is refracted continuously towards the normal. The wave therefore bends back towards the vertical, which is why the paths in the mantle are curved rather than straight.

At the mantle-outer core boundary the density and the wave speed change abruptly, so the wave is partly reflected at the boundary and partly transmitted. The partly reflected waves return to the surface on the far side, which is how the presence and depth of the core boundary are detected.

Inside the outer core the density and the wave speed increase with depth again, so the transmitted wave is refracted continuously and its path curves again, this time with the opposite sense of curvature to the mantle path, because the wave is now bending away from the vertical.

content.text: After a patient had been treated for lung cancer, no tumours were detected in an X-ray image of the lungs.
The doctor has now recommended that the patient have a whole-body PET scan.

Part (i): write down, for each technique, the radiation used, how that radiation is produced, and where the source sits relative to the patient. The differences fall straight out of that list, and you need two of them.

Part (ii): begin from the clinical fact given in the stem - a negative X-ray does not rule out the cancer. Then give a limitation of X-rays, an advantage of PET, and one further reason a whole-body scan is specified rather than a scan of the chest alone.
For part (ii) the three marks are for the three separate pieces of justification, not for elaborating one of them at length.

items: An X-ray image uses X-radiation produced in an X-ray tube with the source outside the body, whereas a PET scan uses gamma rays produced by positron-electron annihilation with the source inside the body. A second valid difference is that a radiograph is a single projection, while a PET scan needs two coincident detections in a ring of detectors.

A conventional X-ray images soft tissue poorly and its resolution may be too coarse to show a tumour that has shrunken during treatment, so a negative X-ray does not exclude cancer. PET detects regions of unusually high metabolic activity regardless of tumour size, and a whole-body scan reveals whether the cancer has spread.

content.text: Part (i). An X-ray image is made with X-radiation produced in an X-ray tube: a heated filament emits electrons that are accelerated onto a metal target, converting some of their kinetic energy into X-rays. The tube sits outside the patient and a single projection is recorded. A PET scan is made with gamma rays produced when a positron, emitted by an injected radiopharmaceutical, annihilates with an electron inside the patient. So the differences are the type of radiation (X-rays against gamma rays), the mechanism of production (an X-ray tube against particle annihilation), and the position of the source (outside the body against inside it). A further difference is that a radiograph needs one detection, while a PET image is built from coincident pairs of detections in a ring of detectors.

Part (ii). The X-ray result is not conclusive. X-rays are absorbed in proportion to density, so soft tissue produces very little contrast, and after treatment the tumours may have shrunk below the resolution limit of the technique, so a clear image does not mean a clear patient. A PET scan does not rely on density contrast at all: it relies on the fact that the injected radiopharmaceutical is taken up faster by tissue with unusually high metabolic activity, which is characteristic of a tumour, so a 'hot spot' is detected even for a small lesion. Because the patient is scanned over the whole body, the scan also shows whether the cancer has metastasised, which a chest X-ray could not. These three points together justify the doctor's recommendation.

Part (i): two tissues that look identical to the eye must still produce different data if they are to be distinguished. Ask what the machine actually measures about each nucleus, and what property of grey and white matter sets that measurement.

Part (ii): resonance means efficient energy transfer between two things that share a natural frequency. Work out the frequency at which the protons precess in the strong field, then ask what happens when a pulse of exactly that frequency is applied to them.
Finish by following the signal. The pulse is short, so something must change once it stops, and that change is what the receiver detects. Each of those steps is a separate mark.

items: The T1 and T2 relaxation times depend on the water content of the tissue, and grey and white matter have different water contents, so their relaxation data differ and the analysis shows where each is located.

The strong field aligns the protons, which precess at the Larmor frequency. A radio pulse at that same frequency makes them resonate, so they absorb the pulse's energy and precess in phase. As they relax they emit radio waves, and the change in the net field they produce is measured and processed into the image.

content.text: Part (i). The signal in an MRI scan is not a density measurement; it is a measurement of how long the excited nuclei take to return to their original alignment, the T1 and T2 relaxation times. Those times depend on how freely the water molecules move in the tissue and therefore on the water content. Grey matter contains more water than white matter, so the two give different relaxation times. Analysing the relaxation data from each volume element produces an image on which the two tissue types are clearly distinguished, even though they have similar densities and would be almost indistinguishable on a CT scan.

Part (ii). Resonance is the efficient transfer of energy between two systems that share a natural frequency. In the very strong magnetic field of the scanner the hydrogen nuclei align with the field and precess about it at the Larmor frequency, $f = \dfrac{\gamma B}{2\pi}$, where $B$ is the field strength. A radio frequency pulse at exactly that frequency is then applied; because the pulse frequency matches the precession frequency the protons resonate, absorbing the energy of the pulse and precessing in phase with one another. When the pulse stops the protons relax back towards their original alignment, and in doing so emit radio waves. The change in the net magnetic field they produce is picked up by the receiver, and the data are analysed by a computer to build the MR image.

content.text: Assess the impact of advances in understanding of waves on the development of imaging technologies. Support your answer using THREE examples.
Three examples are required, and the earlier parts of this question hand you exactly three: ultrasound, X-ray imaging and the endoscope. Use all three rather than substituting others.

For each one, name the specific wave property or behaviour the technique depends on - reflection and refraction at a tissue boundary, differential absorption by density, and total internal reflection in an optical fibre.

Then make the judgement the verb 'assess' demands: say whether advances in understanding waves have been the limiting factor in developing these technologies, and justify that claim from the three examples.
Ultrasound, X-ray imaging and endoscopy all depend directly on understanding of wave behaviour, and each was made possible by that understanding.
Understanding waves has had a significant impact on the development of imaging technologies.

Ultrasound is a technology based on the understanding of reflection and refraction of sound waves when they strike a boundary between two different tissues. Knowledge of the relative intensity of the incident and reflected sound wave is essential if an image is to be constructed of the two tissues.

X-ray images are produced using differences in absorption of X-radiation by different body tissues. Understanding that more dense tissues such as bone absorb more X-radiation is therefore essential if a contrast is to be produced between tissues on the X-ray.

The endoscope is used to transmit light inside the body so real time images of internal structures can be seen. The structure of the optical fibres used to transmit the light is based on understanding that light is totally internally reflected when it strikes a boundary between a more optically dense and a less optically dense medium at an angle greater than the critical angle.

content.text: The apparent brightness of a star depends on its absolute magnitude and its distance from Earth.

Part (i): rearrange the distance-modulus equation so that the apparent magnitude is the unknown, then substitute the absolute magnitude and the distance in parsec. Track the sign of the $5\log$ term as you go, and check that the answer is plausible for a bright star.

Part (ii): two methods are needed and each must be outlined, not just named. One measures an angle directly; the other infers the distance from the brightness only after the intrinsic luminosity has been obtained from the spectrum. State the extra step the second method needs.

If you are unsure which quantity the modulus relates, remember the defining idea: apparent magnitude measures the brightness received at Earth, absolute magnitude the luminosity the star actually emits.

items: Trigonometric parallax, where the angular shift $p$ of a nearby star against the background stars is measured over six months and $d = 1/p$ in parsec; and spectroscopic parallax, where the apparent magnitude is measured, the absolute magnitude is estimated from the spectral class and luminosity class, and the distance modulus is then used. The period-luminosity relation for Cepheid variables, followed by the distance modulus, is also acceptable.

content.alt_text: Graph of relative brightness against time for a binary system showing a shallow narrow dip repeated either side of a much deeper and broader dip that reaches about 0.4 of the original brightness.
Graph of relative brightness against time for a binary system showing four deep narrow dips of equal size, each falling to about 0.5 of the original brightness for a very short time.

content.text: Part (i): these dips are eclipses, and an eclipse is a geometric accident. Ask what has to be true about the orientation of the orbital plane relative to our line of sight, and how common that is among binary systems.

Part (ii): compare the two curves feature by feature before interpreting anything. Look at the depth of each dip within a curve, whether the dips are equal to each other, and whether the bottom of a dip is flat or pointed.

Then ask, for each feature, what it tells you about the two stars - specifically their radii and their temperatures. A flat-bottomed dip means one star is completely hidden for a time; a pointed dip means the eclipse is momentary.

items: These are eclipsing binary systems, and a regular eclipse is only seen when the plane of the orbit lies in our line of sight. In most binary systems the orbital plane is inclined to that line, so the stars never pass in front of one another as seen from Earth, no eclipse occurs, and no change in brightness is detected. At very great distances the small change may also fall below the detection limit.

The left-hand curve is a system whose two stars have different radii and different temperatures: the deep dip is the cooler, dimmer star being eclipsed, the shallow dip is the hotter, brighter star passing in front, and the flattened bottom shows that one star is totally hidden for a period of time. The right-hand curve is a system of two stars of the same size and temperature, so the total eclipse is momentary and every dip is identical.

content.text: Part (i). Both curves show a regular, repeating drop in brightness, which is the signature of an eclipsing binary: one star periodically passes in front of the other from our point of view. That requires the plane of the orbit to lie very nearly in our line of sight. In most binary systems the orbital plane is inclined at a large angle to that line, so the stars never cross in front of one another as seen from Earth, no eclipse occurs and the apparent brightness stays constant. A second, weaker reason, also acceptable, is that at very great distances the small change in magnitude may be smaller than the detection limit.

Part (ii). Left-hand curve: two different eclipses appear, one deep and one shallow. The deep one is the cooler, less luminous star being eclipsed by the brighter star, and the shallow one is the hotter, brighter star being eclipsed by the dimmer one. The bottom of the deep dip is flat, meaning one star is completely hidden for a period of time, and that can only happen if the two stars have different radii.

Right-hand curve: every dip is identical in depth and has a pointed, V-shaped bottom. Identical dips mean the two stars are at the same temperature, so each eclipses the other equally. A momentary total eclipse means the stars have the same radius, so neither is hidden for a finite time. The system is therefore two stars of equal size and equal surface temperature.

content.text: Explain how emission spectra and absorption spectra are produced by specific types of celestial objects.
Handle the two spectra separately rather than trying to describe them in one pass. For an emission spectrum, ask what has to happen to an electron for it to emit a photon of a particular wavelength.
For an absorption spectrum, ask what has to be happening to light as it passes through a cooler layer, and which electrons take up the energy as it passes.

The question asks for the spectra to be explained 'by specific types of celestial object', so name the kind of object as well as the process for each - hot gas for one, and a dense source seen through a cooler outer layer for the other.
Emission nebulae and quasars produce emission spectra; stars with cooler outer layers over a dense core produce absorption spectra.

Emission spectra are produced when electrons within atoms are excited to higher energy levels. When these electrons return to ground state they release photons of particular wavelengths. In space, emission nebulae are heated by nearby hot stars, and quasars also produce emission spectra superimposed on continuous spectra.

Absorption spectra are produced when atoms absorb particular wavelengths as light passes through them. Electrons absorb particular wavelengths to 'jump' to higher energy levels, and the wavelengths correspond to differences in energy levels.

Cores of stars tend to produce continuous spectra, and as this light passes through the outer layers of the stars particular wavelengths are absorbed, depending on the temperature and the atoms or molecules present. Most stars therefore produce absorption spectra.

content.text: Part (i): W and the Sun are both marked on the H-R diagram, so compare their positions. Spectral class tells you which is hotter, and the two curves then tell you which temperature matches which curve. Look at both the height of a curve and where its peak lies.

Part (ii): for each star read three things off the H-R diagram - its spectral type, its position relative to the main sequence, and its luminosity compared with the Sun's. Then ask what each of those implies about the size of the star and about the fusion reaction running inside it.

Watch for the combination that the question is really testing in (ii): a star that is cooler than another yet equally luminous can only be much larger, because the radiated power depends on area as well as on temperature.

items: Curve A. W is a class B star and so is much hotter than the Sun, which is class G; it therefore emits more energy overall and its peak lies at a higher frequency.

W is on the main sequence, so it is fusing hydrogen into helium, and it is hot and luminous. Z is well above the main sequence, so it is past the main sequence and is fusing heavier elements; it is cooler than W but of similar luminosity, so it must be much larger than W.

content.text: Part (i). On the H-R diagram W lies on the main sequence near spectral class B while the Sun lies near class G. Moving left along the sequence means a higher surface temperature, so W is much hotter than the Sun. Wien's law places the peak of the spectrum at a frequency proportional to temperature, and the Stefan-Boltzmann law means a hotter body radiates more power per unit area. Curve A is both taller, that is of greater intensity at every frequency, and peaked further to the right, that is at a higher frequency, than curve B. Curve A is therefore the hotter star, W, and curve B is the Sun.

Part (ii). W is on the main sequence, so its energy comes from fusing hydrogen into helium - for a star as massive and dense as a class B star, most likely through the CNO cycle. Z is plotted well above the main sequence, so it has left it and is fusing heavier elements. Z lies to the right of W, class K against class B, so it is cooler, yet its luminosity is comparable to W's. Since $L = 4\pi R^2\sigma T^4$, a cooler star can match the luminosity of a hotter star only if it is much larger. Z is therefore a giant, far larger than W, and its greater size more than compensates for its lower surface temperature.

content.text: Assess the impact of the development of space-based telescopes on the understanding of celestial objects.
The verb is 'assess', so relate a feature of the instrument to a gain in understanding, then weigh it against the limitations. Build the list feature by feature.
The features to look for are what the atmosphere does to light both before and after it reaches the mirror, and what can be done about combining two telescopes whose mirrors are far apart.
Do not forget the counter-argument - cost, size, and the impossibility of servicing or upgrading a telescope in orbit - and finish with an overall judgement rather than a list of benefits.
Space-based telescopes avoid atmospheric absorption and distortion, so they can detect new wavebands, achieve better resolution, and be combined into very long baseline interferometers.
The development of space-based telescopes allows astronomers to avoid a number of problems associated with ground-based telescopes.

Space-based telescopes are above the atmosphere and so they are able to detect wavebands that are normally absorbed. This includes X-rays and infra-red. Being able to detect these wavebands gives astronomers more detail about stars and galaxy structure.

Space-based telescopes do not experience atmospheric distortion and so can achieve better resolution images with a smaller mirror. This allows the telescopes to better identify astrometric binaries and measure motions and distances of stars using parallax.
Linking a space telescope and a ground telescope can create a very long baseline interferometer that further improves resolution, particularly for radio waves, used to study galaxy structure.

Space-based telescopes are therefore a very valuable tool for astronomers studying celestial objects. However, costs and logistical problems mean that ground-based telescopes will always have an important role.

content.text: Polonium-218 is an unstable isotope that can decay to either lead-214 by alpha decay, or astatine-218 by beta decay.
How could a Wilson Cloud Chamber, or similar device, be used to distinguish between alpha decay and beta decay?
A cloud chamber does not measure energy; it makes the track itself visible. Ask what the track looks like for each type of particle.
Alpha particles are far more strongly ionising but much less penetrating than beta particles, so the two leave tracks of different length and thickness in the same vapour.

For the calculation, write the balanced decay equation and remember that the mass defect is the mass of the starting nucleus minus the sum of the masses of the products. The masses given are nuclear masses, so no electron masses are involved.

Alpha particles produce short, thick tracks of closely spaced droplets, because they ionise strongly but have a short range in the vapour; beta particles produce long, thin, sparsely ionised tracks. The appearance of the track distinguishes the two decays.

The alcohol vapour in a cloud chamber is supersaturated, so any ionisation track condenses into a line of visible droplets. The two radiations differ in both ionising power and range. An alpha particle is strongly ionising but is stopped after a short distance, giving a short, thick trail, while a beta particle ionises weakly and penetrates much further, giving a long, thin trail. So the appearance of the track identifies which decay is occurring.

The mass of a polonium-218 nucleus is 218.00897 u, the mass of a lead-214 nucleus is 213.99981 u, and the mass of an alpha particle is 4.00260 u. Calculate the energy released by this alpha decay.
$E = 9.8\times10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$, equivalent to $6.1\,\mathrm{MeV}$.
The decay is $^{218}_{84}\mathrm{Po} \rightarrow {}^{214}_{82}\mathrm{Pb} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$.

Equivalently, using $1\,\mathrm{u}\,c^{2} = 931.5\,\mathrm{MeV}$, the same answer is $E = 0.00656 \times 931.5 = 6.1\,\mathrm{MeV}$. The two must agree: $9.8\times10^{-13}\,\mathrm{J}$ is the SI value and $6.1\,\mathrm{MeV}$ the nuclear-physics value. A common error is to subtract the alpha particle mass from the polonium mass without adding it to the lead mass, which gives the wrong sign for the mass defect.

content.text: An instrument uses a beam of neutrons with a wavelength of 0.2 nm to study the structure of new materials.
Explain why this beam of neutrons is useful in determining the structure of materials.

Neutrons carry no electric charge, so they are not deflected by the electrons and protons in the material and can penetrate deep into it; and their wavelength of $0.2\,\mathrm{nm}$ is comparable with atomic spacings, so beams diffracted from neighbouring atomic planes are resolved and produce diffraction patterns that reveal the arrangement of atoms.

Converting the wavelength from nanometres to metres is the step most often dropped, and it costs a mark. The neutron mass is $1.675\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$, about 1839 times the electron mass, so a neutron of a given wavelength travels far more slowly than an electron of the same wavelength.

For the explanation, two independent features are needed and each must be linked to the experiment. First, neutrons are electrically neutral, so they interact only weakly with nuclei and are neither deflected nor absorbed by the electron cloud; this lets them pass into the bulk of a material instead of scattering only off its surface. Second, $0.2\,\mathrm{nm}$ is of the same order as the spacing between atoms and is some thousands of times shorter than visible light, so a neutron beam is diffracted by the planes of atoms in a crystal. Because the wavelength is fixed, only lattice spacings satisfying the diffraction condition produce peaks, so scanning the angle maps the structure of the material.

The spectroscope revealed discrete spectral lines, which showed that electrons can only occupy certain fixed energy levels, leading Bohr to propose stable orbits.

The Rutherford model of the atom consisted of a positive nucleus and surrounding electrons; however it was not known how the electrons were arranged, or how they were prevented from radiating their energy.
The spectroscope allowed scientists to identify the characteristic spectrographic lines of different elements, including hydrogen.
These lines caused Bohr to hypothesise the existence of stable and fixed orbits for the electrons, since it suggested that there were fixed gaps between the available energy levels.
Without the spectroscope Bohr would not have made this hypothesis and would not have developed his model of the atom.

content.text: In 1927, Davisson and Germer reported the results of an experiment in which they fired electrons at a crystal of nickel and observed how the electrons were scattered.

The conclusion has to be justified by the result, so state the observation first, an interference or diffraction pattern among the scattered electrons, and then the conclusion that this observation forces.
For the significance, ask which specific weakness of the Rutherford-Bohr model the wave picture removes. The model had fixed orbits but could not explain why only those orbits were allowed.
de Broglie's idea is the link: if the electron is a wave standing in its orbit, then only orbits in which a whole number of wavelengths fits are possible.

items: (i) The electrons formed an interference pattern after passage through the nickel crystal, and since interference is a phenomenon observed only with waves, they concluded that electrons also behave as waves.

(ii) The Rutherford-Bohr model had fixed electron orbits but could not explain why only those orbits were stable. Knowing that the electron is a wave resolves this, as de Broglie showed: the electron can only exist in orbits in which it experiences constructive interference, that is, a whole number of wavelengths.

content.text: (i) The experiment scattered a beam of electrons off a nickel crystal and measured the angles at which they were detected. The result was a set of intensity maxima and minima, an interference pattern. Interference and diffraction are wave phenomena, so the only conclusion consistent with the result is that electrons have a wave nature and a wavelength, which contradicts the assumption that they behave purely as particles.

(ii) The significance is that the wave picture supplies the quantum condition the Rutherford-Bohr model was missing. In that model the orbit radii were postulated and their existence was left unexplained. If the electron's path is a standing wave, then a whole number of wavelengths must fit around the orbit, so $2\pi r = n\lambda$, which quantises $r$ and therefore quantises the energy. The observed diffraction pattern is direct evidence for exactly this wave character, so the model can now explain why only particular orbits are stable.

content.text: Construct a truth table for this logic circuit.
Write the logic in words before building the table. Work out what the NAND gate actually receives, and what the bubble on its output then does to that result.
A bubble on the output of a NAND gate inverts the result, and a NOT gate on an input inverts that input, so the net effect of the two inversions must be accounted for with De Morgan's theorem.

For the second sub-part, remember that logic levels are set by a voltage threshold and not by a fixed value, so each of the three measured voltages must be classified as high or low before the reading can be compared with the table.
The circuit is an OR gate: $A=0,B=0 \rightarrow C=0$; $A=0,B=1 \rightarrow C=1$; $A=1,B=0 \rightarrow C=1$; $A=1,B=1 \rightarrow C=1$.
Each input first passes through a NOT gate, so the NAND gate receives $\overline{A}$ and $\overline{B}$ and produces $C = \overline{\overline{A}\cdot\overline{B}}$.

The double inversion cancels, so the circuit performs the OR function: the output is 0 only when both inputs are 0, and 1 for each of the other three combinations. Filling in the four rows gives the truth table stated in the answer.

content.text: A student measured the inputs and output from an unknown gate and obtained the following readings: 0.2 V, 4.0 V, 4.5 V. Is it valid to substitute this gate for the logic circuit? Justify your answer.

No, it is not a valid substitute. Taking $0.2\,\mathrm{V}$ as low and $4.0\,\mathrm{V}$ as high gives $A=0$, $B=1$ and a high output, which agrees with the table. But only one of the four input combinations was tested, and many different gates give 1 for that one combination, so the other three rows must be checked before the gate is accepted.

Logic levels are decided by a threshold, with anything below about $2.5\,\mathrm{V}$ read as low, or 0, and anything above read as high, or 1. The measured $0.2\,\mathrm{V}$ is therefore $A=0$ and the $4.0\,\mathrm{V}$ is $B=1$, while the $4.5\,\mathrm{V}$ output is high, so $C=1$. Reading the $A=0,B=1$ row of the truth table also gives $C=1$, so the measurement is consistent with the original circuit.

It is still not a valid substitute, because consistency with one row is not proof of the logic function. An OR gate, a NAND gate, an XOR gate and an XNOR gate all give 1 for the single combination $(0,1)$, and the other three combinations were never applied. Each of the remaining input pairs must be tested and its output compared with the table before the unknown gate can be accepted or rejected.

content.text: Explain an application for this circuit.

A fire or over-temperature alarm. As the air heats, the PTC thermistor's resistance rises, the voltage across the diode rises, and when it reaches the relay's operating voltage the relay contacts close and switch a separate sounder or lamp circuit. The variable resistor sets the temperature at which this happens.

Because the thermistor is fixed at $10\,\mathrm{k\Omega}$ in this sub-part, the only quantity that varies is the setting of the variable resistor, so the diode voltage lies between $3.0\,\mathrm{V}$ and $8.2\,\mathrm{V}$. Applying the divider the other way round, across the variable resistor, would give $0.8$ to $6.0\,\mathrm{V}$ and is the common error.

For the application, a PTC thermistor's resistance increases as the temperature rises, so heating increases the fraction of the supply across the thermistor and therefore raises the diode voltage. When that voltage reaches the value at which the relay coil pulls in, the relay contacts close; the relay then switches a separate, higher-current circuit such as a sounder or an alarm lamp, so the small sensing circuit never has to drive the alarm directly. The variable resistor selects the temperature threshold. Other acceptable applications include an over-temperature cut-out in an oven and a motor-cooling fan, or a bath or aquarium temperature controller.

content.text: Explain how amplifiers and feedback loops are used in control systems. Support your answer with a diagram.
Define the feedback loop first, saying precisely what travels from the output back to the input, and then say what the amplifier does with the signal that arrives at the summing point.
Negative feedback is the common case: identify what is being subtracted at the summing junction, and what benefit reducing the error gives.
The question asks for a diagram, so a closed loop containing a summing junction, an amplifier, an output and a feedback path must be drawn as well as described.
An amplifier boosts the (usually small) input signal, and a feedback loop returns part of the output to the input so that errors are reduced; negative feedback is most common.

Control systems, such as those in industrial, communications, medical and entertainment applications, use feedback loops (closed-loop systems) and amplifiers to reduce the variations prevalent in open loop systems.
A feedback loop is where part of the output is transmitted back to become part of the input.

Negative feedback is most common in control systems, where the signal is out of phase and is subtracted from the input to reduce gain. This improves performance (gain stability, linearity and frequency response) and reduces sensitivity to parameter variations (manufacture) or environment (temperature or voltage).
Positive feedback (addition to the input) causes instability (hysteresis) and can be used for comparators or oscillators such as in timing circuits.

For the second sub-part, ask what physically sets a floor on the size of a component. There is a limit to how small a piece of matter that performs a reliable switching function can be.
Two further brakes on the doubling are worth naming: the heat generated as more devices are packed onto the same area, and the growing number of connections that must be routed between them.

Miniaturisation: large numbers of transistors and other components can be manufactured onto a single silicon chip, so the device is small, durable and operates at lower energy levels. Equally acceptable: lower production cost, since many components are printed onto one chip instead of being made separately and then assembled onto a circuit board.

Only one advantage is required, but it must be explained. The strongest single argument is the count: even a simple calculation needs many individual transistors, so a discrete transistor computer had to be large, less powerful and less reliable. An integrated circuit builds the same many tiny transistors onto the one silicon chip, which makes the device more compact, efficient and cost-effective. Cost of production is the common alternative framing, since printing many components at once replaces making each one separately and then assembling them onto a board.

content.text: Integrated circuits are used in all modern electronic devices.
Between 1970 and 2015 the number of transistors that an integrated circuit could contain doubled every two years. Explain why this trend is unlikely to continue into the future.

The trend is unlikely to continue because there is a limit to miniaturisation: a component cannot be produced much smaller than an atom. Chips also may not continue to grow larger because of the heat generated by the packed devices and the difficulty of interconnecting them, and at very small separations quantum effects such as electron tunnelling through the components must be considered, since tunnelling destroys the switching behaviour the device relies on.

The doubling of the transistor count every two years came from photolithographic shrinking of the printed features, and three separate limits now bite. The first is geometric: a component cannot be made much smaller than an atom, so the number that will fit in a given area is approaching a ceiling. The second is thermal and interconnect related: as more devices are packed into the same area the heat generated per unit area rises, and the connections needed to carry signals between them become the limiting factor. The third is quantum mechanical: as the separations shrink, electrons tunnel through what should be insulating layers, so the potential barrier that provides switching no longer holds the electrons, and quantum effects must be considered rather than ignored.

content.text: Assess the impact on society of applications of transducers other than thermistors. Use one input and one output transducer to support your answer.

The question demands one input transducer and one output transducer, so choose them deliberately: an input transducer converts a physical quantity into an electrical signal, an output transducer does the reverse.
Each transducer must be tied to an effect on society and not just to an application. The mark is only earned once the consequence for people has been stated.
Because this is an assessment, finish with a judgement about which effect matters most, rather than leaving two unrelated examples side by side.
Solar cells (input transducers) and current meters (output transducers) both have significant impacts on society.
Transducers are used in most electronic circuits and have a significant impact on most areas of society, as shown in the examples below.

Solar cells (input transducers) convert solar energy to electricity, which may then be used in these circuits. This reduces the demand for coal-fired electricity production which reduces $CO_2$ production, benefiting society through reducing global warming risks.
Solar-generated electricity can be used in remote locations where the grid is not available, improving the quality of life of people and giving them access to communications technologies.

Current meters (output transducers) detect and show the current in a circuit to be viewed (by a decision maker) or connected to another circuit (control system). This potentially results in increased safety or more efficient control of systems.
